justification: As a technical editor, the argument this article makes is genuinely good: a single running example (Temperature -> Freezing -> HeatAdvisory) walks a reader from 'covered but wrong' through assertion strength, branch coverage, and boundary values, into mutation testing, killing/surviving mutants by hand once Stryker.NET is shown (with a real, executed failure) not to work against this pillar's file-based programs. Every complexity-adjacent claim I re-derived checks out exactly: Freezing.Classify's ternary is one comparison / two branches, and the two-test version genuinely hits 2 of 2; the three-way severe/Freezing rewrite has two comparisons / four branches and the three tests genuinely hit all four; HeatAdvisory's three tests genuinely miss only the 38 boundary. I ran every quoted primary source down myself (not just trusted the citation): Microsoft Learn's 'branch a/branch b -> 50%' example, the mutant/killed/survived definitions, the equivalent-operator table row, and the 'don't chase 100% mutation score' note are all verbatim and in context; Stryker.NET's introduction sentence is verbatim; Coverlet's README line/branch/method phrase is verbatim; Fowler's 'upper 80s or 90s' / 'suspicious of anything like 100%' and the correctly-attributed Marick 'subtle difference' quote are verbatim. That is real, careful sourcing work, and most of this article would be a clean pass. Two things stop it there. First, and most binding under this rubric: `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/code-coverage.md` does not reliably pass. I ran it eight times across this review (isolated, no other process touching this worktree): three of the eight runs failed, always on the exact same block (`id=killed`, line 705), always because xUnit v3 does not guarantee the print order of `Classify_BelowThreshold_ReturnsFreezing` versus `Classify_AboveThreshold_ReturnsNotFreezing` when both fail inside one `[Fact]` class, and the article hard-codes one specific order as literal expected stdout. A page whose stated premise is 'every coverage number on this page was produced exactly that way' (line 136) shipping one output block that a reader cannot reliably reproduce by copy-pasting is exactly the kind of failing code this rubric caps at 5, and I confirmed the same root cause the AdSense and design critics independently found this round. Second, and not previously flagged: the sentence "a project that showed a client 'extensive JUnit test coverage'" (line 142) puts that phrase in quotation marks and cites Fowler's AssertionFreeTesting bliki for it. I fetched that page's raw text directly (not a summary): the actual sentence is 'The twist is that the company made a big point of using heavy testing with JUnit. Every public method had to have JUnit tests. They proudly showed the client all the tests and the green bar.' The phrase 'extensive JUnit test coverage' does not appear anywhere on that page, in that wording or any close paraphrase presented as a quotation. That is a fabricated quotation attributed to a real, named, linked source, which is exactly what hard rule 1 forbids, independent of the fact that the surrounding two quotations in the same sentence are accurate. Between the unreliable code and the invented quotation, this cannot score above the rubric's 'broken' anchor this round, however strong the underlying argument and structure are.

issues.location: lines 664-701, the `id=killed` csharp run block and its text output block ('A different mutation on the same two-test version...')
issues.problem: The program is correct and its behavior is correct, but the article's literal expected stdout hard-codes `FreezingTests.Classify_BelowThreshold_ReturnsFreezing` failing before `Classify_AboveThreshold_ReturnsNotFreezing`. xUnit v3 does not guarantee the order in which two independent `[Fact]` methods in one class are discovered/reported. I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/code-coverage.md` eight separate times during this review: five passed, three failed, every failure at this exact block with the two failing tests printed in the opposite order (verified by diffing the tool's own expected/actual output). This is not environment noise from other agents' worktrees; each run was isolated and the mismatch is always the identical swap. `docs/ARTICLES_PLAN.md` §3.1's definition of done requires `gate.mjs` (which wraps `run-code.mjs`) to pass, and a block that fails roughly a third of the time is not a passing check, regardless of which run happens to land in `gate.json`.
issues.fixLooksLike: Make the block order-independent before handing off again: either split the two assertions into two separate single-`[Fact]` `csharp run` blocks the way `weak`/`tight`/`fixed` already are elsewhere in the article, or force a deterministic order (e.g. `[assembly: TestCaseOrderer]`/`[TestPriority]`-style ordering already used on the site, if any pillar article does this), or, if xUnit's ordering truly cannot be pinned down cheaply, wildcard the two `[FAIL]` sub-blocks the same way timing lines are already wildcarded elsewhere and say in prose that xUnit does not guarantee which of two simultaneous failures prints first. Re-run `run-code.mjs` at least five times in a row afterward to confirm the flake is actually gone, not just not hit this time.

issues.location: line 142, "a project that showed a client 'extensive JUnit test coverage,' except 'there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests'" (cites Martin Fowler, AssertionFreeTesting)
issues.problem: The phrase 'extensive JUnit test coverage' is presented in quotation marks as Fowler's own words. I fetched the raw page text directly: the actual passage reads 'The twist is that the company made a big point of using heavy testing with JUnit. Every public method had to have JUnit tests. They proudly showed the client all the tests and the green bar. However there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests.' That exact phrase, or anything close enough to justify quotation marks, does not appear anywhere on the page. The second quotation in the same sentence ('there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests') is accurate, which makes the fabricated first half easy to mistake for equally verified. This is a fabricated quotation attributed to a real, linked, named source -- precisely what the editorial brief's hard rule 1 forbids -- not a paraphrase-with-quotes-by-accident, since the actual source material ('heavy testing with JUnit', 'the green bar') was clearly read and could have been quoted or paraphrased honestly instead.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the invented quotation with either the source's actual language (e.g. paraphrase as 'a project that made a big point of heavy JUnit testing and proudly showed a client the green bar') or drop the quotation marks entirely and describe the scenario in the writer's own words, keeping only the quotations that are verbatim ('there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests').

issues.location: line 783, "Fowler's closing line about coverage doubles as the honest summary of everything on this page: 'If a part of your test suite is weak in a way that coverage can detect, it's likely also weak in a way coverage can't detect.'" (cited to Fowler, TestCoverage)
issues.problem: I fetched the raw TestCoverage page directly: that sentence is immediately followed on the page by its own '-- Brian Marick' attribution line, in the same visual/markup form as the correctly-attributed Marick quote two paragraphs earlier in this same article ('I expect a high level of coverage... subtle difference'). The article attributes one Marick quote correctly and the other to Fowler by name, on the same page, about the same person's words. It is also not the page's actual closing content -- the page ends by pointing to a separate Marick essay and to Testivus, not with this sentence.
issues.fixLooksLike: Attribute this sentence to Brian Marick, consistent with the earlier, correctly-attributed quote in the same section (e.g. 'Marick's own closing line doubles as...'), and drop 'Fowler's closing line' since neither the authorship nor the 'closing' framing is accurate.
